opening.say: Picture a point walking around a circle at a steady speed, never speeding up, never slowing down, round and round.
Now ask how high that point is above the middle of the circle at each moment as it goes.
Hold that height in your head, because the sine graph is just that height written down against the angle.

more.say: Say the circle has radius one. Then the point starts at the right, level with the center, so its height is zero.
As it climbs, the height grows until the point sits at the very top, where the height is exactly one.
Then it comes back down through zero, dips to the bottom at negative one, and rises again toward where it began.

plan.setup: Watch the height as the point goes around.
plan.narration: [[circle-appears]]Here's the circle, and the point starts at the right. [[point-climbs]]As it climbs, its height rises and falls. [[full-turn]]After one full turn, it's back exactly where it began. [[graph-repeats]]Same place, same height, so the graph must start over. That's why sine repeats every two pi.
plan.plan:
circle-appears: a unit circle with a point at angle zero on the right, a thin horizontal line marking its height y, which equals sine of theta.
point-climbs: the point moves counterclockwise and a dot traces y = sin theta on a graph beside the circle, rising to one, falling through zero.
full-turn: the point completes angle two pi and lands back at the start, the circle highlighted once around.
graph-repeats: the traced curve y = sin theta draws a second identical wave, with one period marked as two pi.
plan.close: If the point kept going, what would the height be after three full turns?
